title: The Immaculate Conception (8 December)
hookLine: readings from Genesis 3 and the Annunciation
carry: full of grace from the start

cards: Ask a room of people what the Immaculate Conception is, and someone will probably say: it's when Jesus was conceived without a human father. It's an easy mix-up. But that's the virgin birth, a different teaching.
December 8 is about Mary herself, and the first moment of her own life. In the middle of Advent, nine months before her birthday on September 8, the Church stops for a solemnity.
And the readings it chooses go all the way back to a garden.

teach.b: The first reading is Genesis 3. Adam and Eve have eaten the fruit and hidden. God walks in the garden and calls, where art thou?
Then God speaks to the serpent, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed: she shall crush thy head."
She, in that translation, because the Latin Vulgate says ipsa; the Hebrew points instead to the woman's offspring, he or it.
Either way, Catholic tradition hears a first promise here: a woman and her child, and a struggle with evil that ends in victory. Then the gospel jumps to Nazareth.

The angel Gabriel greets a young woman: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." Full of grace translates one Greek word, kecharitōmenē, a form that suggests favor already given and still lasting.

In 1854, Pope Pius IX defined what Catholics had long celebrated: that Mary, from the first instant of her conception, was kept free of original sin, by a singular grace, in view of what her son would do.
Not because she earned it, and not apart from Christ, but as the first fruit of his work.

teach.h: EVE IN THE GARDEN, MARY IN NAZARETH.
teach.b: Side by side, the two readings show a shape: Eve, who reached for the fruit in the garden, and Mary, who would say be it done to me, in Nazareth.

teach.h: FULL OF GRACE FROM THE START.
teach.b: Christian traditions differ here. Orthodox Christians honor Mary as all-holy but generally don't accept the teaching in this defined form, and Protestant churches generally don't teach it.
For Catholics it's a holy day, and in the United States, Mary under this title is the nation's patroness.

how: Catholics keep December 8 as a solemnity, a holy day of obligation in many countries, with readings from Genesis 3 and Luke's account of the Annunciation.

games.q: the Immaculate Conception — tap the pairs.

s: the Immaculate Conception means Jesus was conceived without a human father
that's the virgin birth. December 8 is about Mary's own conception.
the Douay-Rheims 'she shall crush' follows the Latin Vulgate
the Vulgate says ipsa, she; the Hebrew points to the woman's offspring.
the teaching says Mary earned her freedom from sin
it was a singular grace, given in view of what her son would do.

games.q: you're Mary in Nazareth. an angel appears and says, hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. what do you do first?
o: bow at once and say yes.
feel troubled, and wonder what this greeting means.
games.why: Luke says she was troubled and wondered what manner of greeting this could be. her yes comes later, after her own question.

practice: If you pray, say one Hail Mary slowly, aloud or silently; it opens with the angel's greeting and then Elizabeth's before it asks anything, so let each phrase land.
If you don't pray, sit with the greeting itself, full of grace, and think of a beginning in your own life that was a gift, something you didn't earn. Then rest in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Kecharitomene, full of grace. The angel's name for Mary in Luke one: favor already given, and still lasting, kept on December eighth. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: full of grace, favored one; the angel's name for Mary in Luke 1:28.

carryVoice: Your line: full of grace from the start. Not the virgin birth: Mary's own beginning. Day six hundred thirty-five, done.
